1)Department of Chemical and Biological Engineering, Princeton University, Princeton, New Jersey 08544, USA 2)Department of Chemistry, Department of Physics, Program in Applied and Computational Mathematics, Princeton Institute for the Science and Technology of Materials, Princeton University, Princeton, New Jersey 08544, USA

(Dated: 18 April 2023)

ABSTRACT: In this work, we construct distinct ﬁrst-principles-based machine-learning models of CO2, reproducing the potential energy surface of the PBE-D3, BLYP-D3, SCAN and SCAN-rvv10 approximations of density functional theory. We employ the Deep Potential methodology to develop the models and consequently achieve a signiﬁcant computational eﬃciency over ab initio molecular dynamics (AIMD) that allows for larger system sizes and time scales to be explored. Although our models are trained only with liquid phase conﬁgurations, they are able to simulate a stable interfacial system and predict vapor-liquid equilibrium properties, in good agreement with results from the literature. Because of the computational eﬃciency of the models, we are also able to obtain transport properties, such as viscosity and diﬀusion coeﬃ- cients. We ﬁnd that the SCAN-based model presents a temperature shift in the position of the critical point, while the SCAN-rvv10-based model shows improvement but still exhibits a temperature shift that remains approximately constant for all properties investigated in this work. We ﬁnd that the BLYP-D3-based model generally performs better for liquid phase and vapor-liquid equilibrium properties, but the PBE-D3-based model is better suited for predicting transport properties.

## I. INTRODUCTION

High levels of atmospheric CO2 are the primary factor in the ongoing global temperature rise, leading to severe environmental consequences such as rising sea levels and ocean acidiﬁcation.1–4 Carbon capture and sequestration has been proposed as a method to reduce emissions to the atmosphere without compromising energy production. In this approach, the emitted CO2 is captured at its source, transported through a pipeline either as a gas or liquid, and stored underground in porous geologic formations such as deep saline aquifers.5–7 Experimentally studying these processes involves recreating the subsurface conditions of these geologic reservoirs, which can be challenging due to the high temperature, pressure and salinity conditions.8,9 In view of this, molecular simulations can provide detailed insights of these processes, by allowing the calculation of a variety of structural, thermodynamic and transport properties of CO2 under a wide range of conditions. Empirical force ﬁelds provide an eﬃcient way to simulate CO2 molecules, usually consisting of simple functional forms with parameters obtained by ﬁtting speciﬁc experimental data. When applied to conditions close to the ones used in their parameterization, these models can indeed be successful, which explains their widespread use. As an example, models such as EPM210 and TraPPE11,

parameterized to vapor-liquid equilibrium (VLE) experimental data, perform reasonably well for predicting the critical point and coexistence densities.10,12–16 However, due to the empirical nature of these models, they often lack in transferability and may fail when predicting other properties not targeted during model parameterization. For the case of EPM2 and TraPPE, these models fall short in representing two-phase coexistence properties when applied to mixtures of CO2 and water.17,18Most empirical models do not account for polarizability and many-body eﬀects and may depend on implicit error cancellation in describing physical interactions.17,18 Improving upon these empirical models and extending their applicability to mixtures is not straightforward. For instance, the performance on water/CO2 would depend also on the compatibility with the chosen water model and its accuracy for pure water. Factors such as inclusion of many-body eﬀects or polarizability have been considered to increase accuracy of empirical models17,19,20, but that alone might not lead to the desired result. For example, for CO2, a linear and symmetric molecule with zero dipole moment, incorporating polarizability may not be enough to achieve signiﬁcant improvements. Polarizability eﬀects were shown to present a bigger impact in mixtures with polar molecules such as water.20,21

Ideally, to represent interactions in CO2 over a broad range of thermodynamic states, ab initio methods can be used to obtain points on the potential energy surface. Saharay et al. applied density functional theory (DFT) with the Perdew-Burke-Enzerhof (PBE) functional and ab initio molecular dynamics (AIMD) to predict the structure, the dynamics and vibrational modes

of supercritical CO2 in good agreement with experimental results.22,23 Balasubramian et al. later revised these calculations by including an empirical vdW correction to the interaction energy to account for the dispersion forces present in CO2.24 They found signiﬁcant changes in the pair correlation functions, emphasizing the importance of including dispersion corrections into CO2 force ﬁelds.24

Goel et al.25 assessed the accuracy of various functionals in predicting the vapor-liquid equilibrium of CO2 and concluded that PBE and BLYP with D3 dispersion correction perform reasonably well in predicting VLE properties and molecular structure properties. However, the high computational expense associated with such calculations constrains AIMD simulations to timescales of a few hundred picoseconds and system sizes of fewer than a hundred atoms, limiting their applicability. Alternatively, several models have been constructed by parameterizing force ﬁelds to ab initio data. Bukowski et al. developed the many-body symmetry-adapted perturbation theory (SAPT),26 which accurately predicts second virial coeﬃcients. Bock et al. also predicted second virial coeﬃcients in excellent agreement with experimental results by using a four-dimensional potential energy surface ﬁtted to second-order Møller-Plesset perturbation (MP2) theory calculations.27 However, for bulk thermodynamic properties such as VLE, Bratschi et al. has shown that these two models fall short.28 To improve upon these results, Yu et al. developed a physically motivated force ﬁeld ﬁtted to the SAPT energy calculations, which produced accurate predictions of the VLE, density, isobaric heat capacity and diﬀusion of CO2. However, the accuracy of the model relied on empirically scaling the dispersion coeﬃcients parameterized from the SAPT calculations.29 Their subsequent revision to incorporate three-body eﬀects reduced but it did not completely eliminate the need for a scaling factor. Higgoda et al. also generated a force-ﬁeld parameterized to ab initio data by developing a model ﬁt to pair potentials calculated at the CCSD(T) level of theory, yielding improved predictions of the self-diﬀusion coeﬃcient and viscosity relative to other common force ﬁelds, though it is unclear how this model performs for VLE properties.30 Yue et al.31 developed a data-driven many-body model by ﬁtting a model to large sets of one-body and two-body energies calculated with the CCSD(T) level of theory. The model’s predicted second virial coeﬃcients agreed well with experimental results but for the VLE properties, scaling was needed to attain reasonable agreement with experimental results. In order to overcome the computational drawbacks of these existing models and to improve model accuracy and transferability, machine learning (ML) techniques can be applied to construct the potential energy surface and match the accuracy of ab initio methods eﬃ- ciently. Because of their data-driven nature, applicability can be extended to diﬀerent systems and conditions, as long as the training sets selected to develop these models are representative. In this work, we utilize the Deep

Potential (DP) scheme to develop neural-network-based potentials for CO2.32,33 Through this scheme, in order to represent the potential energy surface, a deep neural network is trained to a set of reference energies and atomic forces generated from ﬁrst-principles DFT calculations. The resulting potential energy surface can then be used to perform “deep potential molecular dynamics” (DPMD)33 simulations eﬃciently. DP models trained upon DFT calculations have been shown to achieve accuracies comparable to the reference DFT data for a variety of systems.34–38 Furthermore as a testament to their computational eﬃciency, such models have been used to simulate millions of atoms on timescales of tens of nanoseconds.39

In this work, ML models were obtained for CO2 based on four diﬀerent reference DFT exchange-correlation functionals: the Perdew-Burke-Enzerhof (PBE)40 and the Becke-Lee-Yang-Parr (BLYP),41 both with the D3 dispersion correction,42 the strongly constrained and appropriately normed (SCAN) functional, and SCANrvv10, including long-range vdW interactions from the revised Vydrov-Voorhis (rVV10) nonlocal correlation functional.43 Using these models, bulk liquid densities were ﬁrst calculated in isothermal-isobaric (NPT) ensemble simulations. Direct-coexistence molecular dynamics (MD) simulations were also performed to assess their accuracy in reproducing vapor-liquid equilibrium properties such as coexistence densities, interfacial tension, and vapor pressures. Finally, the self-diﬀusion coef- ﬁcient and viscosity of CO2 were also obtained with the three models. The article is organized as follows. In section II, we discuss the data preparation, construction of the DP models and our simulation and analysis methodologies. In section III, we analyze and assess the results obtained from our models to understand the overall accuracy of these density functionals and DP implementation. Section IV includes our conclusions and potential future investigations.

## II. METHODS

## A. Development of DP models

All models were constructed following the DP methodology.32 For every conﬁguration in the training set, the positions of each atom and its neighbors within a cutoﬀrc were converted to a set of "descriptors" that preserve translational, rotational, and permutational symmetries. To construct the descriptors, a local environment frame is considered for each atom, deﬁned by the speciﬁed cutoﬀradius. A weighting function is also applied, gradually reducing the weight of neighbors that are further way from the center atom and thus removing the discontinuity brought by the cutoﬀradius. The atomic coordinates of each atom and the neighbors within the frame are processed into neural network descriptors that

contain angular and radial information and are invariant for permutations of atoms of the same chemical species, providing a symmetry-preserving representation of the local environment of each atom.33,44 For all models, rc was chosen to be 6 Å. The descriptors then serve as inputs to a deep neural network with three hidden layers each containing 90 neurons to output the atomic energies. The total energy of a given conﬁguration is given by the sum of the individual atomic energies. The atomic forces were obtained by taking the gradient of the energy. The parameters of the neural network are obtained by minimizing the loss function (L), deﬁned as the sum of the square errors of the system energy (∆E) and atomic forces (∆Fi) normalized by the number of atoms. The prefactors pe and pf are tunable parameters, varying during the optimization process.

Four DP models were constructed based on density functional theory (DFT). The ﬁrst two were based on the Perdew-Burke-Enzerhof (PBE) functional40 and the Becke-Lee-Yang-Parr (BLYP) functional41 respectively, both with dispersion correction D3 applied42. The other two were based on the strongly constrained and appropriately normed (SCAN) functional45 and a version of SCAN with long-range van der Waals interactions, SCAN-rvv1043. For the construction of the PBE-D3 and BLYP-D3-based models, the training data were labeled through single point calculations performed with the CP2K46 quantum chemistry software package. For both models, the Goedecker-Teter-Hutter (GTH) pseudopotential47 was used to model the core electrons in the C and O atoms. An energy cutoﬀof 600 Ry for the electron density was used. For the SCANand SCAN-rvv10-based models, the quantum chemistry software package Quantum Espresso48 was used for the single point calculations. Troullier-Martins (TM) pseudopotentials49 were used, with energy cutoﬀs for the Kohn-Sham orbitals of 150 Ry and 240 Ry for the SCAN and SCAN-RVV10-based models, respectively. Dimer potential energy curves for all four DFT methods can be found in the Supporting Information. For all models, conﬁgurations forming the initial training set were obtained from classical MD simulations of bulk liquid states at T=220-300K and P=100 bar for a system of 64 molecules in the isothermal-isobaric (NPT) ensemble, with the TraPPE11 force ﬁeld. Subsequently, these conﬁgurations were labeled through single point calculations using the selected DFT method. Additional conﬁgurations were added to the training set through the active learning scheme DPGEN50 to adequately sample the conﬁgurational phase space. In total, 2,414 and 3,800 conﬁgurations were used to train the PBE-D3 and BLYP-D3-based models, respectively. For the SCAN and SCAN-rVV10-based models, the same 1,301 conﬁgurations were used to construct each training set.

## B. Ab initio Molecular Dynamics Simulations

We validated the PBE-D3 and BLYP-D3-based models by running ab initio molecular dynamics (AIMD) simulations with the respective DFT functionals and pseudopotentials. The CP2K software package46 was used and simulations with a system of 64 CO2 molecules at P=100 bar and T=220-280K were run for 40-50ps. The same energy cutoﬀof 600 Ry was applied. For these calculations, we used 4 Intel Skylake nodes with 2.4 GHz, 128 CPU cores and achieved a performance of approximately 8.3 ps/day for a 64-molecule system. Pair correlation functions obtained from the AIMD simulations are reported in Supporting Information and match well literature data as well as correlation functions obtained from the DP models for the corresponding DFT methods.

## C. Deep Potential Molecular Dynamics Simulations

The LAMMPS package51 with the DeePMD-kit plugin32 was used for all simulations performed with the constructed DP models. For all MD simulations with DP models, a timestep of 0.5 fs was used. Using a single Xeon Broadwell E5-2680 v4 node, with 2.4 GHz and one 1328 MHz NVIDIA P100 GPU, 28 Intel Broadwell e5-2680v4 CPU cores, we were able to simulate a 64-molecule system with a speed of 4.5ns/day.

## 1. Bulk Densities

To calculate liquid densities using the constructed DP models, NPT simulations at P=100 bar and T=220-280K were performed with a system of 512 CO2 molecules. A stochastic velocity-rescale thermostat with a relaxation time of 0.5 ps and 0.05 ps was used to maintain the pressure and temperature, respectively. The simulations were run for 4-5 ns with at least 2 ns of equilibration.

## 2. Vapor-liquid equilibrium

Direct coexistence simulations were performed to obtain vapor-liquid equilibrium properties of CO2. A vapor-liquid interfacial system was generated by expanding an equilibrated liquid box of CO2 along the zdimension to produce a liquid slab in the x-y plane. In the canonical ensemble, simulations were performed with 1024 molecules and the Nosé-Hoover thermostat was applied for temperature control. The interfacial system was equilibrated for at least 1ns and sampled for at least 4ns. The box size was 31 x 31 x 250 Å3 for the PBE-D3 and SCAN-rvv10-based DP models and 26 x 26 x 250 Å3 for the BLYP-D3-based DP model. The distinct box sizes were chosen so as to accommodate suﬃciently large liquid and vapor slabs.

## 3. Transport Properties

The Einstein relationship was used to compute selfdiﬀusion coeﬃcients (D) using the DP models. A condensed phase box at T=220-300 K with 512 molecules was ﬁrst equilibrated through an NPT simulation using the Nose-Hoover thermostat and barostat for temperature and pressure control, respectively. Using conﬁgurations with densities close to the average density obtained from the NPT simulations, NV T simulations were run for at least 1.5ns and the mean squared displacements of the C atoms were obtained. The self-diﬀusion coeﬃ- cient was calculated from the slope of the mean-squared displacement versus time. The shear viscosities were calculated using the Green- Kubo relation:

The NV E simulations for viscosity calculation were run for 4-5ns. The upper time limit for the Green-Kubo integral was chosen to be 500 ps based upon the speed of the decay of the autocorrelation function.

Results for the bulk liquid densities at P = 1000 bar as a function of temperature for each DP model are compared to experimental data in Fig. 1. Tabulated data and statistical uncertainties for this and subsequent ﬁgures can be found in the article’s Supporting Information. We found that on one hand, the DP SCAN model underestimates densities by approximately 10%, while the DP SCAN-rvv10 model, on the other hand, overestimates them by approximately 8%. Densities from the PBE-D3 and BLYP-D3-based DP models agree well

with the corresponding AIMD results. In agreement with a prior study,25 while the PBE-D3 functional underpredicts the bulk liquid densities, the BLYP-D3 functional slightly overpredicts them. Furthermore, the PBE-D3- based model results are comparable to the ones by the SCAN-based model. Overall, for the bulk liquid phase, we ﬁnd that BLYP-D3 functional is better suited for describing the equation-of-state, providing a good description of van der Waals interactions for this condensed phase. These observations of the relative performance of the four diﬀerent DFT methods for equation-of-state data are consistent with the underlying dimer potential energy curves shown in Supplementary Information. Speciﬁcally, the SCAN-rvv10 method provides a deeper potential well, while the SCAN method has a faster decay of the attractions at longer distances relative to PBE-D3 and BLYP-D3. It should be pointed out that the divergences in liquid density values, specially between SCAN and SCAN-rvv10 results, can be due to several sources. For one, the distinct representation of long-range dispersion should be taken into consideration. While SCAN only oﬀers a portion of intermediate-range dispersion interactions representation, SCAN-rvv10 includes long-range vdW interactions. The D3 and rvv10 can be viewed as two complementary approaches to describe long-range interactions in real systems. While rvv10 can be seen as a conceptually simpler approach, both rvv10 and D3 require empirical parts in their representations and have yielded similar results for a study on cluster interactions55. More details about dispersion correction approaches can be found in reviews, such as Ref. 56. Furthermore, the short-range nature of the machine learning models should be contemplated here. While the reference DFT methods might include dispersion corrections, the DP models only consider a local representation within a pre-deﬁned cutoﬀradius. This means that dispersion corrections are only implicitly taken into account in these models, which might lead to discrepancies between the interactions predicted by DP models and the DFT reference methods. As an additional remark on the representation of the bulk liquid phase, we make a note that we have also calculated liquid densities at a lower pressure, that of P = 100 bar. At this lower pressure, we found that DP SCAN fails to reproduce experimental densities, greatly underestimating them, while the other models show behavior similar to that at P = 1000 bar. These conditions are in the general vicinity of the critical point for CO2, making the liquid highly compressible. These results can be found in the Supplementary Information. Given the inadequate description of the liquid phase provided by the SCAN-based model at P = 100 bar, we make use only of the PBE-D3, BLYP-D3 and SCANrvv10 based models in the remainder of this work for the calculations of properties along the vapor-liquid coexistence curve. Speciﬁcally, we evaluated the performance of the DP models for the vapor-liquid equilibrium properties of CO2. Through direct coexistence MD simulations,

Even though no interfacial snpashots were added into the training set of the models, all three DP models were able to simulate a stable interfacial system with a clear separation between the vapor and liquid phases as shown by Fig. 2. For the DPMD BLYP-D3 simulations, when T > 270K, the results from the ﬁt become less representative since the interface starts to lose deﬁnition signaling proximity to the critical point. The discrepancies shown between the AIMD and DPMD results are likely due to the longer simulation times and greater system sizes used in our DPMD simulations. Additionally, the shortrange nature of DP models, lacking an explicit inclusion of long-range dispersion interactions may also contribute to these discrepancies. However, these results still corroborate that PBE-D3 underpredicts coexistence liquid densities while BLYP-D3 slightly overpredicts them. ## IV. CONCLUSIONS

In this work, four distinct DP models ﬁt to the PBE- D3, BLYP-D3, SCAN and SCAN-rvv10 approximations of DFT were constructed for CO2, enabling eﬃcient simulations at ab initio-level accuracy. The PBE-D3 and BLYP-D3 DP models were validated through comparisons with AIMD simulations of both the bulk liquid phase and vapor-liquid equilibrium. Vapor-liquid surface tensions, not previously available from AIMD simulations, were also obtained using these models. DPMD represents a signiﬁcant computational speed enhancement when compared to AIMD, achieving simulation time scales of nanoseconds per wall-clock-day on a single computing node instead of only a few picoseconds

for AIMD. The longer sampling enabled by the eﬃciency of the DP models also allowed calculations of transport properties – speciﬁcally viscosities and diﬀusion coeﬃ- cients. Both BLYP-D3 and PBE-D3-based DP models are in good agreement with AIMD simulations using the corresponding functional, indicating that the models faithfully represent their underlying potential energy function. The small discrepancies observed are likely due to diﬀerent system sizes and time lengths used in DPMD and AIMD simulations, although the lack of explicit longrange dispersion representation in DP models might also contribute to these diﬀerences. For DP SCAN, our results show that it greatly underpredicts densities at the conditions studied, at which the ﬂuid phase is quite compressible. The DP SCANrvv10 model shows signiﬁcant improvement in comparison to DP SCAN, but our results show that SCAN-rvv10 result in stronger interactions, eﬀectively corresponding to a shift in temperature for all properties examined in this work, when compared to experimental results. This suggests that including the long-range van der Waals interactions is important for this system when using the SCAN functional. In closing, our results attest to the DPMD methodology’s eﬃciency and ability to accurately represent the potential energy surface of the DFT exchange-correlation functionals used in this work. Considering that the training data consisted on liquid simulations only, the DP models developed in this work have also shown to be transferable to vapor-liquid equilibrium conditions. Given the limitations of many current models to accurately represent mixtures of CO2 with water, it would be of great interest to test these models in this capacity in future work, as a further evaluation of their transferability. In addition, given the short-range nature of the DP models, the eﬀects of explicitly taking into account dispersion corrections into these models could lead to further improvements and hence be an interesting avenue for future work.

Keywords. Polymer nanocomposites. Small-Angle X-Ray Scattering. X-Ray Photon Correlation

## Abstract

We find that the initial, solvent-cast state of nanoparticles (NPs) in a polymer matrix temporally

evolves during thermal annealing such that, at steady state, NPs maximize their distance from each

other subject to mass balance constraints. The observed timescales for this unexpected structural

reorganization, as probed by small angle x-ray scattering, are temperature dependent and can be

prohibitively large, especially at temperatures around and below 1.2Tg. X-Ray Photon Correlation

Spectroscopy measurements during reorganization reveal that the collective NP dynamics slow

down with annealing at constant temperature; this is accompanied by changes in the low frequency

regime in macroscopic viscoelastic measurements in equilibrated materials. By ruling out other

potential sources for these effects (i.e., electrostatic interactions, adsorbed layers), we attribute

these results to a long-ranged repulsive force between the NPs caused by fluctuations in the

polymer phase, i.e. the “Anti-Casimir” effect proposed by Obhukhov and Semenov.1 Thus, our

results highlight the important role of long-term, slow NP reorganization on the structure and

subsequently the properties of PNCs, even in the case of nominally miscible polymer nanoparticle

hybrids.

## Introduction

Composite materials comprised of nanoparticles (NPs) added to a polymer matrix, termed as

polymer nanocomposites (PNCs), have been intensely studied over the past few decades. These

hybrids can have significantly altered properties relative to the host matrix,2-5 where changes in

mechanical,6-14 thermal,15-18 rheological,19-24 optical,25-28 transport,29-34 and electrical35-37

properties have been observed. While the presence of NPs often improve properties, dramatic

improvements are usually only observed when the fillers are uniformly dispersed in the matrix;

this is likely because the interfacial area allowing for interactions between the polymer and the

NPs is significantly increased with well dispersed NPs relative to their agglomerated analogs. The

generally accepted guiding principle for fabricating PNCs with dispersed nanoparticles is to utilize

polymers with functional groups which mediate the unfavorable interactions between the

(normally) hydrophilic NP and the (usually) hydrophobic polymer. The presence of these

interacting groups lead to the formation of a “bound layer”, comprised of polymer chains

physically adsorbed to the NP surface.38-40 This layer, which prevents NP agglomeration through

the steric stabilization mechanism (where the bound layer screens attractive van der Waals forces

between NPs leading to NP-NP contact), plays an important role in determining PNC rheological

and mechanical reponses,13, 41, 42 e.g., as discussed by Ondreas et al.43 and Zhao et al.6 At high NP

volume fractions, the bound layers on adjacent NPs could connect, leading to the formation of a

bridged network structure with a solid-like mechanical response.13, 44, 45 The idea of steric

stabilization also carries over to PNCs containing polymer-grafted nanoparticles (where polymer

chains tethered to the surface of the NP mediate unfavorable interactions between the matrix and

the NP) where, again, both the dispersion state and formation of a network structure affect the

mechanical and rheological properties.13, 19, 46, 47


<!-- Page 3 -->


3

Hooper and Schweizer studied the equilibrium structure of PNCs as a function of NP volume

fraction and interaction strengths between the polymer and the NP and provided design rules for

NP dispersion in polymers.48, 49 While attaining the equilibrium NP dispersion state is the ultimate

goal, many recent studies have highlighted how different processing conditions lead to different

PNC structures (and hence, potentially, favorable properties). These conditions include choice of

common solvent50-53 and evaporation rates,54, 55 external fields,56-58 and thermal annealing

conditions.59-61 It has been well established that polymer melts also exhibit differences in

properties based on the processing pathway used62, and thus the fact that most initial PNC states

are non-equilibrium, with an initial dispersion state that is highly dependent on the particular

processing pathway and any subsequent annealing is not surprising. Previously, Chen et al. found

that the viscosity of NP filled polystyrene increases with time and only approaches a steady state

after ~100 hours, much longer than chain reptation and bare NP diffusion times.63 They attributed

this to hindered mobility of the chains adsorbed on the surfaces of the NP, a phenomenon which

has attracted recent attention. Jimenez et al.64 and Bailey et al.65 found that the desorption and

exchange of adsorbed chains with the bulk surrounding polymer is dependent on temperature, with

measurable exchange only occurring when the temperature is high enough to activate the

desorption of multiple surface contacts of a chain. On the other hand, Mackay et al., in an attempt

to disperse NPs in a matrix with unfavorable NP-polymer interactions, found that rapid

precipitation provided a secondary protocol for obtaining well dispersed PNCs.66 However, Cabral

and coworkers found that these composites were also temporally unstable as in-situ SANS

experiments showed particle agglomeration over time.67 Thus, even PNCs with well dispersed NPs

evolve over longer than expected timescales.


<!-- Page 4 -->


4

In this work, we focus on thermal annealing and how it affects the temporal evolution of the

structure, dynamics and properties of model PNCs with nominally well dispersed SiO2 NPs.

Generally, thermally annealing removes residual casting solvent which might be present after

ambient drying. Secondly, heating the composite above the polymer’s glass transition temperature

(Tg; usually >1.2Tg ) allows it to equilibrate. Through in-situ SAXS experiments at fixed

temperature, we find that dispersion state of the NPs evolves from a random dispersion to more

correlated structures at timescales which are much longer than the corresponding relaxation times

of the polymer host. The structural evolution is accompanied by a slowdown in the relaxation time

of the NPs as measured through XPCS, indicating that the effective mobility of the NPs in the

matrix slows down significantly on the formation of the ordered state. This effect propagates in

the rheological response as there is significant low frequency reinforcement in the PNCs for the

composite with increasing NP weight fraction, which can be attributed to the formation of a

percolated structure with interacting bound layers. We propose that the evolution of the NP

structure is a consequence of the drying process where the NPs are kinetically arrested due to

increasing viscosity of the polymer phase. In the melt state, repulsive forces due to matrix

fluctuations result in the rearrangement of the NPs into more ordered arrangements with their

spacing being dictated by the volume fraction of the NPs. Thus, utilizing thermal energy to drive

the PNCs to equilibrium results in more ordered structures with slower NP dynamics and better

viscoelastic response.

## 2. Results and Discussion

All the systems we consider in this work are prototypical PNCs where steric stabilization of the

nanoparticles is achieved by a bound layer of polymer on the NP surface. If we consider the case

of P2VP, the strong hydrogen bond that can form between the nitrogen atom on the pyridine ring

and the hydrophilic silica surface is the driving force behind the formation of the bound layer.

Similar hydrogen bonding interactions also stabilize SiO2 NPs in PMA and PEO leading to steric

stabilization of the NPs, preventing irreversible aggregation. As shown in Figure 1A-1C, TEM

confirms the absence of visible aggregation of the 14 nm silica nanoparticles in the three different

polymers used in the study, P2VP, PMA and PEO, reinforcing the notion that nanoparticles are

nominally well dispersed in these composites. This is true for the larger NPs as well. (See

Supplementary Information, Figure S1). Note that the thicker PEO and PMA films from cryo-

microtoming have a large number of visible NPs despite the lower PNC concentrations (Slices are

100-200 nm compared to particle size of 14 nm).

The origins of compressed exponential behavior for the dynamics of NPs dispersed in a polymer

matrix has been a topic of continued discussion. For colloidal gels, Bouchaud and Pitard91

proposed that microscopic stress relaxations lead to the ballistic behavior. The accumulation of

microcollapses leads to an increase in relaxation time with aging time. Cipeletti et al. found that

## 3. Discussion

The previous sections highlighted the non-equilibrium nature of the NP dispersion in a polymer

matrix and how extensive thermal annealing leads to changes in the nanoscale NP organization.

This affects the NP mobility in the matrix as well as the PNC macroscopic properties.

Theoretically, the reorganization of NPs into short-ranged correlated structures would be an

entropically unfavorable process as the configurational entropy of a random dispersion of NPs

would be higher than that of a uniform dispersion of NPs.97 Thus, we believe that a secondary

long-ranged repulsive potential must exist which drives the NPs into their final equilibrium

structures. For block copolymers adsorbed on flat surfaces, Tirrell and coworkers have previously

measured a repulsive force at distances much larger than the coil size of the unadsorbed block (up

to 4Rg),  which is in line with our assumption of a long ranged repulsive potential.98 Qualitatively,

this repulsive potential explains the long range ordering of the NPs as well as the corresponding


<!-- Page 24 -->


24

decrease in mobility of the NPs. In the absence of any force which drives the NPs to obey mass

balance constraints, steric stabilization and bridging between NPs due to bound polymer chains

would be the expected phase behavior, as has been predicted by Hooper and Schweizer.49 Such a

model has been quantitatively used to describe scattering patterns and real space structure in recent

work focused on P2VP/SiO2 PNCs.44 The bound layer preventing contact aggregation between the

NPs and act akin to a short-ranged repulsive potential, the range of which is dictated by the size of

the bound layer. Thus, as long as conditions promoting the formation of a bound layer remain, the

NPs will not be able to move to a state where NP aggregates are the favored state. As indicated

previously, the well accepted size of the bound polymer layer is based on the Rg of the polymer

chain (5.3 nm for 44 kDa), which is lower than the surface to surface spacing at for low weight

fractions (3-10 wt.%; 30, 20 nm) of 14 nm SiO2 NPs. This is also apparent for the dispersion of 50

nm NPs in PEO, as the NP surface to surface spacing for 14 wt.% NPs in PEO is 40 nm which is

again much larger than the Rg of 40 kDa PEO (5.3 nm). (Figure S17)

Thus, a simple argument based on steric stabilization from the bound polymer layer cannot explain

the observations of interparticle spacing at the lowest volume fractions and decreased ballistic

velocity observed through XPCS, the next most obvious origin of repulsive forces comes from the

charged double layer on the surface of the NPs which stabilize it in solution. Qiu et al.99, Meth et

al.100 and Poling-Skutvik et al.101 were able to model the structure of dispersed NPs in a polymer

solution by invoking the surface charge and utilizing the Hayter-Penfold Rescaled Mean Spherical

Approximation (HPRMSA)102 to fit the equilibrium SAXS curves. However, Meth et al.100 observe

the apparent collapse of the charged double layer during the process of drying, with the appearance

of a scattering pattern similar to what is observed for aggregated nanoparticles as more of the


<!-- Page 25 -->


25

solvent evaporates. Such an observation was also made by us in our studies (see for example,

Figure S9), but annealing at elevated temperatures reverses this phenomenon with time. While

electrostatic repulsion seems like a plausible explanation for the development of the resulting NP

structure, recent experiments in our group have shown that this aging phenomenon occurs in

PEO/NP mixtures with added salt, even in cases where the Debye length is on the order of a few

Angstroms. As the debye length governs the range of interaction, this surface charge induced effect

also seems unlikely to be relevant in this context.51, 53

In the absence of any other argument, the only other explanation which is able to explain most of

the other observations comes from work by Obukhov and Semenov.1 They predicted that

fluctuations in the polymer phase would result in a long ranged (longer than a few monomers)

repulsive force (termed as the anti-Casimir effect) between objects in a polymer melt. In the limit

of long chains, these forces scale as a (n = -3) power law of the ratio of the NP size to the NP

separation (for infinitely long chains) and can thus be operative even at distances of 54 nm, which

is the mean spacing between 14nm NPs at a 3 wt.% in PMA.  At the simplest level, the repulsive

force can explain the observation of NPs following the contraints of mass balance, as well as the

reduction in XPCS derived ballistic velocity, as the motion will be based on a force balance on a

particle. As the magnitude of the force is likely dependent on the chain length, we expect changes

in the degree of correlation with changing molecular weight of the matrix. This is indeed observed,

as the hard-sphere volume fraction of the SAXS fits changes from 0.02 for a molecular weight of

23 kDa to 0.20 for 4 wt.% 14 nm NPs in 96 kDa PMA (Figure S15). This further lends credence

to a chain size fluctuation mediated repulsive force which determines structure, dynamics and

properties in equilibrated PNCs. An important note here is that the formalism for the anti-Casimir


<!-- Page 26 -->


26

force is based on non-interacting spherical inclusions in a polymer matrix. It is not well understood

how the bound polymer layer would influence the manifestation of the force, and remains an open

question.

## 4. Conclusions

We show that NPs well dispersed in a polymer matrix during solvent casting evolve significantly

over time until they reach an equilibrium associated with the loading of the NPs, and the polymer

molecular weight. The timescales for structural reorganization at temperatures around 1.2Tg can

take weeks to reach its final form for 14nm SiO2 NPs dispersed in PMA, making these timescales

prohibitively large, in a system with relatively low Tg and MW. For systems with less mobility

(e.g. P2VP, PS), an equilibrium is likely to never be reached at all, leaving PNCs to be annealed

to arbitrarily rearranged states. The structural reorganization is also accompanied by a concomitant

slowing down in the dynamics of the NPs in the matrix, as seen through X-Ray Photon Correlation

Spectroscopy (XPCS) as well as on the macroscopic viscoelastic response. After extensive

annealing of the PNCs, significant low frequency reinforcement is observed for the composites

and a steady state zero-shear viscosity cannot be achieved within the frequency windows studied.

The changes in low frequency reinforcement is dependent on the NP loading, as samples with low

loadings of NPs still show liquid-like viscoelastic response but with a significantly increased

viscosity. We attribute the structural reorganization to a repulsive force between the NPs due to

fluctuations in the polymer phase. This highlights the important role thermal annealing plays in

determining macroscopic properties, and it also provides insight into the difficulty in comparing

data from similarly fabricated materials which are treated in different manners, as a “true

equilibrium” might not have been reached.

for one hour on a hot plate at 60 oC with 0.5 wt.% Irganox to help reduce degradation in subsequent

steps. For the composites, the NPs were then added via micropipette to the desired loading and

stirred for another hour at 60 oC. The samples were then probe sonicated for three minutes (cycling

two seconds on, one second off), then cast in a Teflon dish at 60 oC in an oven at -5 inHg for one

hour to quickly evaporate solvent without agitation from bubbling. The samples were then left in

the vacuum oven for one day at room temperature to remove any residual solvent.

Samples were molded into open metal plates for the in-situ SAXS and XPCS experiments, with

the minimum amount of temperature and time exposure necessary to melt the samples into the

plate. This required ~30 seconds at 60, 80, and 150 oC for PMA, PEO, and P2VP composites,

respectively. Ex-situ experiments on “as cast” versus quickly molded samples showed little to no

change in structure due to this step. Sample preparation for rheology experiments necessitated

molding into 4 mm disks with a thickness of ~700 μm using a vacuum mold on a hydraulic press


<!-- Page 32 -->


32

at 80 oC. Even though the sample was exposed to an elevated temperature for 1 hour, no difference

in structure between the as cast and molded samples were observed at this temperature.

Thermal Properties

Differential Scanning Calorimetry (DSC)

A TA Instruments Discovery DSC was used for thermal property measurements. The instrument

was calibrated with a sapphire disk for heat capacity and indium for temperature and enthalpy.

Fragments of a disk (~10 mg) were loaded in to aluminum pans and accurate weight measures

were obtained with the TGA. Annealed samples loaded in to the aluminum pans were run under a

nitrogen environment with a ramp rate of 2 oC /min and a temperature modulation of 1.27 oC for

60 seconds while cooling from 80 oC to -20 oC. Prior to the cooling step, the pans were equilibrated

at 80 oC for 1 hour. Glass transition temperatures estimated from the first derivative of the

reversing heat capacity (Cp,rev) and are reported in the Supporting Information.

Thermogravimetric analysis

A TA Instruments thermogravimetric analyzer was used to measure the final weight fraction of

SiO2 NPs in the composites. The instrument was calibrated with Nickel and Alumel for Curie point

temperature calibrations and standardized weights provided by TA Instruments. 5-10 mg of sample

were loaded on to a platinum pan and heated to 700 oC under O2 flow with a ramp rate of 10

oC/min. Terminal steady state was achieved well before the 700 oC limit and the final mass

obtained was used to estimate final NP loadings in the PNCs.


<!-- Page 33 -->


33

X-ray Scattering

Small angle x-ray scattering (SAXS) was performed on a laboratory system at Columbia

University (Ganesha, SAXSLAB) with a Cu KB source (λ = 1.54 Å), a spot size of ~200x200 µm,

a Pilatus 300k detector and a variable sample-to-detector distance which enables the instrument to

cover a q range of 0.005-1.2 Å-1. Scattering experiments were done at room temperature (exposure

time per configuration of 600 seconds) as well as on a Linkam temperature stage (exposure time

of 30s for each time point) for in-situ thermal annealing measurements, both under constant

vacuum (~9E-3 mbar). In-situ thermal annealing experiments were performed at 80, 100, 120, 150

and 190 oC for PMA based PNCs. 2D scattering patterns were integrated using SAXSLAB’s

saxsgui software, as well as pyFAI python packages, to obtain I(q) data. I(q) fits to the Percus-

Yevick hard sphere model were either done with a custom python script or SASView. Additional

SAXS, as well as XPCS, measurements were performed at Argonne National Laboratory’s

Advanced Photon Source on the 8-ID beamline, details of which are noted later.

Electron Microscopy

Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) was performed at NYULMC on an FEI Talos 120C

TEM. Before imaging, the PEO and PMA PNCs samples were cryo-microtomed using a Leica

Ultra UCT Microtome at -80 oC. P2VP samples were microtomed at room temperature on the same

microtome without the cryo attachment. The resulting ~100 nm sections were placed on Formvar-

coated, 400 mesh copper grids and imaged on the TEM at room temperature.

Small Angle Oscillatory Shear

Small Angle Oscillatory Shear (SAOS) experiments were done using a TA Instruments DHR-3


<!-- Page 34 -->


34

strain-controlled rheometer with 4mm parallel plates. Samples were loaded at 60 oC at a gap height

of 700-800 μm, presheared and the axial force was allowed to equilibrate before lowering the

temperature to the lowest temperature to be studied. Axial force control was maintained through

the duration of the experiment. Prior to running frequency sweeps (ω = 0.1 to 100 rad/s), strain

amplitude sweeps (γ = 0.1 to 10%) were conducted at each temperature to determine the linear

viscoelastic regime. The strain amplitude chosen at each temperature was well within the linear

regime. Master curves were generated by time-temperature superposition (shifted to 60 oC).

X-Ray Photon Correlation Spectroscopy (XPCS)

X-Ray Photon Correlation Spectroscopy (XPCS) experiments were conducted at sector 8-ID-I at

the Advanced Photon Source (APS, Argonne National Laboratory). 7.35 keV coherent x-rays were

used in the experiments, which resulted in an accessible q-range of 0.0025 to 0.063 Å-1. X-rays

incident on the sample were attenuated to avoid beam damage on the sample. The size of the beam

incident on the sample was 5 x 15 μm. Intensity autocorrelation functions with annealing time

were obtained at a set temperature (dependent on sample) as a function of waiting time to track

the evolution of NP dynamics. To also avoid beam damage, the beam was rastered around the

sample with no overlap between spots which were exposed to the x-ray beam prior to the current

measurement. Two-time correlation functions were calculated to ensure that we are sampling

homogenous dynamics across one intensity autocorrelation function and not heterogenous

dynamics which are changing over the measurement time. Calculation details and a representative

two-time plot are shown in Figure S18.

# De intransigentes a socialistas. Las proyecciones políticas de las lavanderas del Manzanares (1868-1936) *

From Intransigents to Socialists: The Political Projections of the Washerwomen of the Manzanares (1868-1936)

Renee Congdon Universidad de Princeton rcongdon@princeton.edu ORCID 0000-0001-9842-1679

Recibido el 25 de septiembre de 2025 Aceptado el 9 de enero de 2026 BIBLID [1134-6396(2026)33:1; 207-242] http://dx.doi.org/10.30827/arenal.v33i1.34998

RESUMEN

Este artículo examina la militancia política de las lavanderas del Manzanares en Madrid, desde principios del Sexenio Democrático (1868-1874) hasta el inicio de la Guerra Civil Española. Basado en fuentes periodísticas del momento, examina la participación disputada de este grupo en varios movimientos políticos, empezando con el de los republicanos “intransigentes” y siguiendo después con su afiliación con el Partido Socialista Obrero Español (PSOE) y la Agrupación Femenina So­ cialista. Además, avanza una teoría sobre la función social del lavadero como incubador crucial de la militancia socialista femenina. También aborda las reacciones de distintos sectores de la sociedad burguesa ante las iniciativas de estas obreras politizadas, analizando la retórica empleada para des­ legitimarlas tanto en la prensa política como en ámbitos culturales como el teatro. Finalmente, se cuenta cómo el legado político de este grupo fue neutralizado y borrado mediante varios mecanismos estratégicos de la cultura hegemónica del momento.

Palabras clave: Lavanderas. Proletariado femenino. Agrupación Femenina Socialista. Movilización política. Protesta popular. Pablo Iglesias Posse. Republicanismo. Sexenio Democrático.

## ABSTRACT

This article traces the political militancy of the washerwomen of the Manzanares River in Madrid, from the Sexenio Democrático (1868-1874) to the onset of the Spanish Civil War. Drawing

on contemporary newspaper sources, it explores the contested participation of this group in various political movements, beginning with the “intransigent” republicans and moving on to the Spanish Socialist Workers’ Party and the Women’s Socialist Group. Additionally, it advances a theory regar­ ding the social function of the washhouse as a crucial incubator for female socialist militancy. The article also addresses the reactions of different sectors of bourgeois society to the initiatives of these politicized workers, analyzing the rhetoric employed to delegitimize them both in the political press and in cultural spheres such as the theater. Finally, it recounts how the group’s political legacy was neutralized and erased through various strategic mechanisms of the hegemonic cultural apparatus of the time.

Key words: Washerwomen. Female Proletariat. Women’s Socialist Group. Political Mobilization. Popular Protest. Pablo Iglesias Posse. Republicanism. Sexenio Democrático.

1.—Introducción

En los análisis históricos de los movimientos obreros y la lucha de clases, el obrero fabril ha ocupado casi siempre un lugar central, entendido como una figura emblemática de la solidaridad proletaria y la conciencia revolucionaria. Aunque los trabajadores varones han captado la mayor parte de la atención en la historiografía laboral, la figura de la obrera revolucionaria también ha logrado abrirse paso en el imaginario cultural español, en parte gracias a obras literarias canónicas como La tribuna de Emilia Pardo Bazán. Sin embargo, este énfasis en la fábrica como espacio paradigmático de la formación de la clase trabajadora ha tendido a eclipsar otros espacios fundamentales de organización proletaria, en particular aquellos ligados a oficios tradicionalmente feminizados.

El lavadero se cuenta entre ellos. Aunque hoy pueda evocar asociaciones con el trabajo doméstico no remunerado, en su contexto histórico el lavadero constituyó un centro importante de trabajo asalariado femenino y de acción colectiva. A pesar de su importancia, ha recibido relativamente poca atención crítica en el ámbito de la historia del trabajo (Tatjer, 2002; Sarasúa, 2003). Este artículo busca llenar este vacío, demostrando que el lavadero, al igual que la fábrica, ha funcionado


<!-- Page 3 -->

ARENAL, 33:1; enero-junio 2026, 207-242

como un núcleo clave de la movilización obrera y el desarrollo de la conciencia de clase, particularmente para algunos de los grupos de trabajadoras más marginados y precarizados en el Madrid de finales del siglo xix y principios del siglo xx.

Aunque se han publicado pocos trabajos dedicados específicamente a la movilización política de las lavanderas, este artículo se inserta en una tradición historiográfica amplia y consolidada sobre la protesta popular y la politización de las clases obreras en la Europa moderna. En este marco, la ya canónica noción de “economía moral”, formulada por E. P. Thompson, ha sido fundamental para el análisis histórico de formas de protesta popular y colectiva como los motines de subsistencia, habitualmente asociadas al horizonte del Antiguo Régimen. En el caso español, sin embargo, diversos estudios han mostrado que estas prácticas más “tradicionales” de protesta informal persistieron a lo largo de otras épocas posteriores, con un protagonismo importante en la Restauración española, donde coexistieron con otras modalidades de acción colectiva como la huelga (Arriero, 1984; Gil Andrés, 1995; González Calleja, 1998; Lucea Ayala, 2009).

La participación de las mujeres obreras en las protestas populares de la Res­ tauración ha sido asimismo objeto de una extensa atención historiográfica (Kaplan 1982; Ramos Palomo 1986; Radcliff 1993; Lucea Ayala 2002). Gran parte de esta literatura se ha centrado, no obstante, en la participación femenina en protestas callejeras vinculadas a la economía doméstica, como los motines de subsistencia, en contraste con su menor presencia en la política partidista o sindical formal. Al mismo tiempo, trabajos como los de Kaplan y Radcliff han contribuido a pensar la politización de las mujeres obreras no como una derivación secundaria de la politización masculina, sino como un proceso aparte articulado en torno a lógicas y lenguajes propios. En este marco, Radcliff advierte que incluso los gremios fe­ meninos con un mayor privilegio social y cultural, como el de las cigarreras, han sido “marginados o malentendidos en el lenguaje de la política”, por lo que “la experiencia de otras mujeres de clase trabajadora probablemente haya sufrido un destino similar” (1993: 101) 1.

Partiendo de esta observación, el presente artículo se dirige hacia otro colectivo de trabajadoras cuya experiencia política ha recibido hasta ahora poca atención crítica: las lavanderas del Manzanares. Al enfocar el análisis en este grupo, se propone una relectura de los procesos de politización de los gremios femeninos más precarizados durante la España de la Restauración. Además de reconstruir su trayectoria militante, el análisis se detiene en los mecanismos cotidianos de poli­ tización articulados en torno al espacio del lavadero, identificando el intercambio oral femenino como una práctica central en la formación de una conciencia de clase atravesada por cuestiones de género.

En este sentido, sostengo que el entorno exclusivamente femenino del lavadero funcionó como un espacio privilegiado de sociabilidad y circulación de la palabra, favoreciendo la progresiva politización de las obreras que trabajaban allí. A partir de aportes antropológicos sobre el habla de las mujeres, el artículo examina, en primer lugar, testimonios orales recogidos en los años noventa por la Asociación Cultural La Poza de Pozuelo de Alarcón, en los que las entrevistadas subrayan la centralidad del lavadero como espacio social y comunicativo en la vida cotidiana femenina durante el primer tercio del siglo xx. Estos relatos locales se ponen luego en diálogo con el contexto madrileño más amplio, a partir de fuentes legales y pe­ riodísticas que permiten situar el Manzanares como un foco recurrente de agitación social y protesta popular desde finales del siglo xviii hasta comienzos del siglo xx.

El artículo se detiene en la progresiva formalización de las lavanderas madri­ leñas como sujetos políticos, desde los años iniciales del Sexenio Democrático (1868-1874) hasta el primer tercio del siglo xx. Su primera incursión en los círculos políticos establecidos se localiza en un manifiesto firmado por tres lavanderas y publicado en El Combate, en el que el colectivo se alinea explícitamente con los sectores republicanos “intransigentes” del momento. Esta intervención se inscribe en la historiografía existente sobre la movilización republicana femenina durante el Sexenio Democrático y la Restauración (Espigado Tocino, 2005; Anchorena Morales, 2025), tradicionalmente centrada en mujeres de posición socioeconómica más elevada. El caso de las lavanderas permite ampliar este marco, incorporando trayectorias de politización femenina propias de los sectores más precarizados del mundo obrero femenino.

El análisis se desplaza después hacia la actividad política de la Sociedad de Lavanderas y Planchadoras, sindicato fundado en 1902 que estableció alianzas formales con el Partido Socialista Obrero Español (PSOE) y con la Agrupación Femenina Socialista. Esta dimensión sindical pone de relieve la participación sos­ tenida de las lavanderas madrileñas en el activismo obrero organizado y permite situar su trayectoria dentro de una historia más amplia de la movilización de las mujeres trabajadoras en el socialismo de comienzos del siglo xx, tal como han señalado estudios previos (Capel Martínez, 2008; del Moral Vargas, 2010).

Por último, el artículo analiza las reacciones adversas que esta militancia provocó entre sectores de la élite política y cultural burguesa, que recurrieron a retóricas clasistas y sexistas para deslegitimar el activismo de las obreras. Estas respuestas se inscriben en un entramado más amplio de discursos hegemónicos que buscaban neutralizar la amenaza que representaban los movimientos de eman­ cipación obrera de la época. Esta contraofensiva se desplegó en distintos espacios culturales, desde la política y el periodismo hasta la literatura y el teatro.

Para captar la magnitud de esta reacción discursiva, concluiremos nuestro análisis con un enfoque en el género chico, cuya popularidad en Madrid coincidió —tanto en términos cronológicos como geográficos— con momentos clave de la movilización obrera. Mientras en espacios teatrales como el Barbieri las lavan­

2.—“Allí era el congreso”: El lavadero como espacio alternativo de producción

de saberes

Como argumenta la sociolingüista Deborah Jones, las mujeres pertenecemos a una comunidad lingüística aparte, “con competencias lingüísticas y disposicio­ nes que nos son propias” (Jones, 1979: 194) 2. No obstante, el tipo de habla que se produce en estos círculos exclusivamente femeninos ha sido históricamente menospreciado, etiquetado como chisme. Al definirse por su proliferación en es­ pacios íntimos fuera del alcance del oído masculino, este tipo de habla femenina siempre ha suscitado sospechas, percibido como malicioso o, en el peor de los casos, blasfemo, estrechamente vinculado al Diablo y sus artimañas (Federici, 2018: 41-42). Sin embargo, este tipo de habla femenina ha sido reevaluado en años recientes por académicas feministas, quienes han redefinido el llamado “chisme” como un “lenguaje de la intimidad” (Jones, 1979: 194) 3 que no solo forma la base de una cultura oral femenina sino que también y, de manera crucial, ha funcionado como un “camino de acceso al conocimiento” (Adkins, 2017: 3) 4. En efecto, si bien durante siglos se ha criticado el chisme por considerarlo banal o malintencio­ nado, académicas como Maryann Ayim han afirmado que el “malestar general” que provoca “no concuerda con su caracterización de charla trivial (small talk). Quienes temen el chisme saben demasiado bien que, lejos de ser ‘pequeña’, se trata de un tipo de conversación capaz de arruinar reputaciones, minar relaciones, alterar radicalmente el equilibrio de poder e, incluso, en algunos casos, derribar instituciones venerables” (Ayim, 1994: 96) 5. El chisme contiene, por tanto, un potencial radical de transmisión de saberes e intercambio de información, repre­

Es precisamente este potencial radical el que se manifiesta en enclaves pro­ tegidos del habla femenina como lo ha sido el lavadero, ya que el chisme históri­ camente ha florecido en contextos de trabajo doméstico femenino (Jones, 1979: 194) 6. Como artefacto de una sociedad patriarcal que históricamente ha relegado a las mujeres las labores de limpieza y mantenimiento del hogar, el lavadero emerge como un espacio dual y contradictorio: producto de una imposición patriarcal, pero a la vez forjado como un “espacio vedado” para los hombres, lo cual impli­ caba que “las relaciones sociales y conversaciones establecidas en el lavadero… por desarrollarse al margen de su área de influencia,… escapaban a su control y conocimiento” (Cantero Fernández, 2015: 176). Es en este espacio donde las mu­ jeres hallaban un foro para expresar sus quejas, compartir inquietudes y establecer lazos de solidaridad a través de una comunidad de habla íntima y exclusivamente femenina. Entre el susurro de secretos, las peticiones de consejo y las quejas amar­ gas que circulaban en ese foro, sostengo que se activa un potencial de discurso político que termina por desbordar los límites del lavadero. En efecto, cuando una lavandera chismosa señala en secreto a una vecina que pasa y describe en voz baja la paliza que le propinó el marido celoso anoche, está entablando también un diálogo implícito sobre la violencia doméstica y la subordinación histórica de las mujeres 7. Cuando se lamenta con amargura de que sus clientas le han escamoteado el pago de una semana de trabajo, también está reflexionando sobre la precariedad de su situación laboral y, por extensión, sobre la explotación capitalista de la clase trabajadora. Y cuando narra con rabia su último enfrentamiento con el guardia municipal asignado a su tramo del río, está tejiendo, de forma oral, un relato sobre

of wrecking reputations, undermining relationships, radically shifting the balance of power, and even in some cases bringing down venerable institutions”.

6.  Madrid cuenta con una rica tradición de espacios sociales destinados explícitamente al intercambio de información oral, a menudo con una carga política. Diversos espacios de la capital, conocidos como mentideros, funcionaron como núcleos de discurso político masculino, y en oca­ siones incluso se les llegó a denominar como lugares de chismes. No obstante, para los fines de este artículo, entenderemos el chisme como un término que alude tradicionalmente al habla femenina, tal como lo plantea Deborah Jones.

Nunca tal hiciera, pues las lavanderas todas le dieron tal cantidad de bofetadas y arañazos, que le pusieron la cara hecha un mapa. Y menos mal que acudieron en su ayuda, que sino nadie le salva de llevarse un remojón, dadas las intenciones que tenían de tirarlo al río” (El Correo Gallego, 08/03/1927: 4).

Asimismo, en contextos urbanos como el de Madrid —donde cientos de lavanderas asalariadas trabajaban codo con codo— la inquietud que generaban el lavadero y las conversaciones que allí circulaban se veía intensificada por el origen proletario de sus trabajadoras, especialmente en un momento en que las clases obreras emergían como actores clave de la agitación social en su lucha por la emancipación. La posibilidad de que las lavanderas que frecuentaban las ori­ llas del Manzanares pudieran estar tramando en secreto contra sus empleadores —o incluso contra sus propios maridos— se convirtió así en una preocupación implícita en torno a estos espacios de reunión exclusivamente femeninos, que constituían uno de los escasos foros de socialización de mujeres en la sociedad española de la época.

Si bien las reivindicaciones feministas del chisme en la literatura académica son relativamente recientes, las mujeres que frecuentaban estos espacios no ig­ noraban el potencial subversivo inherente al diálogo que allí se entablaba. Esto se evidencia en las entrevistas realizadas tanto a lavanderas profesionales como a amas de casa que lavaban en el lavadero público de Pozuelo de Alarcón antes de su destrucción parcial durante la Guerra Civil española. Dichas entrevistas fueron llevadas a cabo en la década de los noventa por la Asociación Cultural La Poza en un esfuerzo por preservar la memoria histórica de la vida cotidiana en el pueblo en los años previos a la guerra 9.

Al preguntárseles en términos generales de su vida cotidiana antes de la guerra, las mujeres de Pozuelo mencionan con notable frecuencia el lavadero público del pueblo. Algunas de las entrevistadas trabajaban como lavanderas remuneradas, mientras que muchas otras eran amas de casa que lavaban allí la ropa de sus fa­

Algunos de estos temas también se ven reflejados en Fuimos indómitas: un recorrido por los oficios desaparecidos de las mujeres de Madrid, de Victoria Gallardo Romera (2021).

9.  Pozuelo de Alarcón constituye un caso particularmente interesante en lo que respecta a la memoria histórica de las lavanderas. Antes de la Guerra Civil, Pozuelo albergaba una numerosa población obrera, y el lavadero público era un espacio reconocido de socialización femenina. Pozuelo era especialmente conocido por sus lavanderas profesionales, ya que los madrileños acomodados solían preferir contratar a lavanderas procedentes de las comunidades periféricas de Madrid, donde la calidad del agua era superior. Devastado por la guerra y despoblado debido a la evacuación de sus habitantes durante ese periodo, Pozuelo fue posteriormente designado como “Pueblo Adopta­ do”. Sin embargo, desde la década de 1980 hasta la actualidad, el nivel económico de Pozuelo ha experimentado un notable crecimiento, convirtiéndose hoy en una de las ciudades más acomodadas del país. Las entrevistas citadas aquí fueron realizadas en el marco de un esfuerzo comunitario por preservar los recuerdos de las formas de vida que Pozuelo una vez conoció.

milias. Sin embargo, de manera invariable, las mujeres entrevistadas aludían a lo que ocurría en el lavadero con una mezcla de humor y secretismo, riendo al relatar cómo era aquel espacio. Varias entrevistadas hasta revelan los diversos apodos que usaban para referirse al lavadero, apodos que, pese a las risas cómplices que los acompañan, dejan entrever la astuta conciencia que tenían sobre el potencial radi­ cal y subversivo del discurso que allí se intercambiaba. Una vecina comenta, por ejemplo, que “[c]harlaríamos de todo… la que estaba [en la] orilla chascabas con ella y con la otra y allí se comentaba las cosas (ríe)… (riendo) allí era el congreso” (“Entrevistas a Martín de Rozas…, 1999: 51-52). Otra, de modo similar, explica a la entrevistadora que solían llamar a ese espacio “el parlamento”, “porque… todas las cosas del pueblo allí salían en el parlamento… allí se desataban (risas) todos los pleitos” (“Entrevistas a Losa Pérez…”, 1997: 188-189).

En estos comentarios, soltados entre risas cómplices y sonrisas pícaras, las mujeres de Pozuelo llevan a cabo un gesto carnavalesco al comparar el espacio exclusivamente femenino del lavadero público —generalmente considerado un lugar humilde— con las más altas instituciones de poder y justicia. Asimismo, se posicionan, en esta imaginación alternativa, como las árbitras de los asuntos más importantes del pueblo, llegando incluso a denominar estos asuntos “pleitos”, término directamente asociado con las instituciones gubernamentales y el proceso judicial. En efecto, apelativos como estos reflejan la posición privilegiada que el lavadero ocupaba en el mundo social de estas mujeres, a pesar de su concepción dentro de la sociedad masculina como un espacio periférico. Aunque siempre mencionados entre risas, los apodos que las mujeres de Pozuelo utilizaban para el lavadero público nos brindan valiosas pistas sobre la función social de este espacio, que surgió como un foro de discusión femenina de carácter paraoficial. Al deno­ minar a este lugar “el congreso” o “el parlamento”, las entrevistadas participan en una imaginación colectiva de un mundo distinto, empleando un gesto casi barroco para hallar su propio centro de poder en los márgenes de la sociedad patriarcal.

Las narrativas orales que se han tejido en el espacio del lavadero pueden enten­ derse, por tanto, como espacios dinámicos de construcción, debate e intercambio de conocimiento, particularmente en un momento histórico en que las mujeres, especialmente aquellas de origen popular, se encontraban excluidas de los espa­ cios institucionales destinados a tal fin. Como afirma Maryann Ayim respecto a la exclusión histórica de las mujeres de lugares como la universidad, “siempre han existido otras vías hacia el conocimiento, menos veneradas pero a menudo más eficaces. El chisme es una de ellas” (Ayim, 1994: 85) 10. En este sentido, el lavadero puede concebirse como un foro emblemático de esta vía alternativa de conocimiento. 3.—A orillas del río: El discurso subversivo y la lucha sostenida por control del

Manzanares

El río Manzanares, antes de su canalización a mediados del siglo xx, constituyó durante siglos el principal espacio de trabajo de las lavanderas profesionales de Madrid. Si bien resulta difícil precisar el número exacto de mujeres que se dedica­ ban a este oficio, se sabe que a mediados del siglo xviii el Manzanares contaba con al menos “1.142 bancas y 24 banquillos” para el lavado, según los archivos de la Hacienda municipal (Sarasúa, 2003: 63). Que las miles de mujeres que diariamente lavaban en sus orillas utilizaban este espacio no solo para trabajar sino también como lugar de socialización e intercambio de información queda evidenciado en las ordenanzas municipales que regulaban este espacio.

En efecto, los lavaderos del Manzanares tenían fama de ser el núcleo del dis­ curso de las mujeres proletarias y llegaron a ser concebidos explícitamente como una amenaza al orden establecido. Ya desde el siglo xviii, las preocupaciones sobre la naturaleza disruptiva del discurso que emanaba de estos lavaderos llegaron a plasmarse en decretos legales, los cuales abordaban directamente la inclinación de las lavanderas hacia un habla transgresora y amenazante a la paz. El siguiente decreto, publicado en Madrid en 1790, da cuenta de ello:

LAVANDERAS. Las que concurren al río de Manzanares, sus ayudantes y criados se abstengan de proferir juramentos, palabras obscenas é indecentes, y de injuriar de obra ó palabra á las personas que pasan por las márgenes del rio ó por los lavaderos, ni salgan de estos ni sus bancas á gritar y causar rumores ni quimeras, pena á los contraventores de que se les destinará por quince dias á las obras públicas, y si fueren mugeres por igual tiempo á la reclusión de San Fernando (Memorial literario instructivo, 1790: 34).

Que la proclama se dirija específicamente a la naturaleza transgresora y des­ bordante del habla de las lavanderas es revelador, dejando entrever que, desde la perspectiva del Estado y de las autoridades, el discurso de estas obreras represen­ taba una amenaza tangible al orden establecido y, por ende, debía ser controlado y censurado.

Lejos de ser un hecho aislado, los decretos y ordenanzas legales dirigidos a la regulación de los lavaderos del Manzanares fueron frecuentes a lo largo de los siguientes siglos. Dos ediciones consecutivas de las Ordenanzas municipales de Madrid, publicadas en 1832 y 1892, dedican capítulos extensos a la gobernanza,


<!-- Page 10 -->


ARENAL, 33:1; enero-junio 2026, 207-242

RENEE CONGDON 216

control y mantenimiento del orden en los lavaderos del Manzanares. Entre los más de treinta artículos incluidos en este capítulo de la edición de 1892, muchos versan sobre la supervisión de la actividad que se desarrolla a orillas del río, incluyendo la vigilancia y regulación del comportamiento y el discurso de quie­ nes allí trabajaban. Uno de estos artículos, por ejemplo, exigía a las lavanderas obtener permisos oficiales del alcalde y portar en todo momento una “cartilla” de identificación indicando el número del lavadero en el que estaban empleadas (Ordenanzas municipales, 1892: 119). Varios otros artículos del capítulo abordan directamente la importancia de mantener el orden y el decoro en los lavaderos, ordenando la asignación permanente de guardias, inspectores y agentes policiales a lo largo de ambas orillas del río con el fin de garantizar la disciplina y el orden:

Art 550: Para la debida vigilancia y buen gobierno de los lavaderos de las dos riberas habrá un Inspector de policía urbana con el número de guardias que reclame el servicio de los mismos (Ordenanzas municipales, 1892: 119-120).

Otro artículo, de forma semejante, decreta que “los dueños, colonos ó arren­ datarios de lavaderos tendrán especial cuidado de que dentro de los mismos se conserve el mayor orden y no se cometan abusos…denunciando al Teniente de Alcalde del distrito ó al Inspector de la ribera cualquier falta ó delito que se co­ meta” (Ordenanzas municipales, 1892: 119).

La estricta regulación de las orillas del Manzanares mediante decretos y or­ denanzas desde al menos el siglo xviii en adelante refleja la percepción popular de este espacio como un núcleo de desorden, disturbios y alteraciones en el centro urbano. En efecto, la ubicación de los lavaderos a lo largo del Manzanares impli­ caba que las lavanderas estaban a la vista pública en el corazón de un Madrid en plena expansión urbana. Por ello, estas preocupaciones sobre el comportamiento y el habla de las lavanderas probablemente reflejan su alto potencial para atraer la atención pública, así como el posible efecto dominó que podría desencadenarse si las lavanderas decidieran rebelarse.

El potencial disruptivo de los lavaderos era altamente conocido en todos los sectores de la sociedad madrileña, e incluso inspiraba chistes y refranes populares. Un ensayo satírico publicado en La Nación en 1852 ofrece un ejemplo represen­ tativo de la connotación que este espacio poseía en el imaginario popular del mo­ mento. Titulado “Influencias locales”, el texto comienza observando que “parece que cada sitio o demarcación de las afueras de esta corte tiene propensión á ser teatro de ciertos y determinados delitos” (La Nación, 11/1/1852). A continuación, el autor ofrece ejemplos, señalando la asociación entre el canal y “los suicidios”, la Puerta de Segovia y sus accidentes de carruajes, y los “solitarios sitios de San Bernadino” y los duelos (La Nación, 11/1/1852). Antes de concluir, el autor dedica un extenso párrafo final a los infames lavaderos del Manzanares, empleando un tono sumamente sardónico:

[…] los lavaderos desde la Florida, en toda su estension, hasta el puente de Toledo son la escepcion de la regla: cualquiera que niegue la amabilidad y sensatez de las lavanderas, su lenguaje elocuente y escogido, cierta propensión al silencio, humildad y carácter placentero, con un trato afable y cariñoso; cualquiera, re­ petimos, que niegue tan relevantes cualidades, quiere levantar á todas 11 un falso testimonio (La Nación [Madrid. 1849], 11/1/1852).

El pasaje funciona como un claro y mordaz comentario irónico sobre la repu­ tación popular de las lavanderas, dejando abundantemente claro las connotaciones precisas del Manzanares y de sus lavanderas en el paisaje urbano del Madrid del siglo xix.

Las orillas del Manzanares, como hemos visto, constituían un conocido foco de discurso disruptivo. Las lavanderas, protagonistas de estos incidentes, adquirieron en el imaginario burgués la reputación de alborotadoras empeñadas en perturbar la paz. Esta reputación, leída desde abajo, permite trazar los inicios de lo que iden­ tifico como una historia olvidada de lucha subalterna. Recopilando relatos sobre la creciente participación de las lavanderas en círculos políticos y movimientos obreros, podemos seguir su avance hacia una participación política más formal, así como el surgimiento de una conciencia de clase y una identificación explícita con ideologías como el republicanismo federal “intransigente” y, más adelante, el socialismo.

4.—“Hemos de hacer una manifestación que sea sonada”: El manifiesto de 1870,

o la entrada formal de las lavanderas del Manzanares en el escenario político madrileño

A mediados de noviembre de 1870, Madrid vibraba con fervor político. El príncipe italiano Amedeo Ferdinando Maria di Savoia había sido elegido por el general Prim como candidato probable para ser el próximo monarca de España, un monarca que, por primera vez, sería elegido por el Parlamento español. A medida que se acercaba el día del voto, los columnistas políticos llenaban las páginas de los periódicos con debates sobre la entrada de este extranjero en el gobierno es­ pañol. Entre estas columnas, el 12 de noviembre, el diario madrileño El Combate

11.  En el Madrid del siglo xix, era común que los transeúntes se plantaran en los puentes de Segovia o Toledo a gritarles a las lavanderas. Con frecuencia, la frase empleada fue “¡Todas, todas!”. El cronista D. Antonio de Trueba relata que esta frase, al ser gritaba, solía provocar una cadena de insultos y maldiciones por parte de las mujeres que lavaban (de Trueba, 1866: 552). Aunque de Trueba pretende, con inocencia simulada, desconocer el significado de la expresión, parece tratarse de una abreviatura de un estribillo misógino más largo: “todas sois unas putas, todas, todas”.

publicó una carta redactada por lectores del periódico, expresando su oposición vehemente al reinado de Amadeo.

Lo llamativo de esta carta, sin embargo, es que no fue redactada por escrito­ res políticos ni por pensadores burgueses, sino por tres humildes lavanderas del Manzanares. Las autoras, que aseguran hablar en nombre de todas sus compañeras, expresan su enérgica oposición a la inminente instauración del rey Amadeo I. Su firme postura antiamadeísta se alinea con la ideología radical de los republicanos federales “intransigentes”, un grupo que, tras la proclamación de la monarquía en la Constitución de 1869, rompió con los republicanos “benevolentes”, protagonizando una serie de levantamientos armados y una intensa actividad política y periodística durante los años del Sexenio Democrático. Los “intransigentes” representaban, así, el sector más radical del ala progresista del Congreso de los Diputados en ese momento. Al vincularse con esta facción, las lavanderas no sólo denuncian la imposición de un monarca extranjero, sino que se sitúan explícitamente dentro del imaginario político revolucionario del momento. Afirman:

Hace días que está resuelto entre nosotras labanderas del rio de Madrid ó sea del Manzanares, no consentir que se llame Rey de España el italiano amadeito dichoso ó sea el hijo del escomulgado: para esto nos emos juntado en esta tarde de frio todas las que tenemos aquel oficio, y convenidas hacemos presente, que ya que vuestro periódico es el más valiente y más querido nuestro, nos dirigimos a ti para que aprovechando nuestro pensamiento y deseo, hagas un apunte largo á nuestro nombre que exprese con la energía de que eres capaz, nuestros propósitos ya que las que tenemos marido no podemos conseguir de ellos que se hubieran armado ya, pero esperemos que lo harán y combatirán á la entrada en esta corte de un Rey tan repugnante como aborrecido (El Combate, 11/12/1870: 3).

La carta se abre presentando el lavadero como un espacio de deliberación política, al relatar cómo “todas las que tenemos aquel oficio” se reunieron “en esta tarde de frío” para redactarla. Esta escena sitúa la orilla del río como un parlamento informal, uno de los pocos espacios públicos accesibles a mujeres de clase trabajadora excluidas de la política institucional. Lejos de ser un lugar de chismes triviales, el lavadero emerge aquí como un crisol de alfabetización po­ lítica y agencia colectiva, en el cual las lavanderas leían periódicos, debatían los acontecimientos del momento y articulaban demandas compartidas. El manifiesto revela no sólo una conciencia cívica aguda, sino también el uso estratégico de un espacio de trabajo feminizado como plataforma de intervención política por parte de un grupo marginado en los relatos históricos dominantes.

Las autoras de la carta también especifican que eligieron dirigirla a El Combate en particular “ya que vuestro periódico es el más valiente y más querido nuestro”. Esta afirmación evidencia que el colectivo no solo tenía acceso a diversos perió­ dicos políticos de la época, sino que mostraba una preferencia marcada por uno de los más militantes y radicales que circulaban en ese momento. En comparación
